To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) oviposition by a gall-forming wasp triggers the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in Eucalypt leaves; (2) the ROS production and other responses to ovipostion may lead to gall formation; (3) gall development is associated with cell division in the leaf tissue; (4) the oviposition fluid is the main trigger for gall development; and (5) the ovipostion fluid contains a protein that stimulates cell division.
oviposition by gall-inducing insects induces a complex physiological and transcriptional response in the host plant.
oviposition by gall-inducing insects induces a rapid oxidative burst and phenolic accumulation, which are reflected in the transcriptomic changes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the physiological changes that take place in plants following insect egg deposition, and the transcriptional changes that occur in plants in response to insect eggs.
the physiological and transcription responses of the plant to oviposition and the egg-induced stimuli that promote gall development.
the physiological and molecular responses of a host plant to egg deposition and oviposition by a galling wasp, Lepto-cybe invasa.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the oviposition of the gall wasp Leptocybe instigates the plant defence system in the host tree Eucalypt, however, the plant defence system is re-programmed to support gall formation.
the egg and the oviposition fluid of Leptocybe induce physiological changes and transcription reprogramming in Eucalypt that are involved in the formation of galls.
oviposition induces a rapid and complex transcriptional and physiological response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
oviposition by Leptocybe wasps induces a rapid response in Eucalypt hosts, which may be directed towards defence or gall formation.
oviposition of Leptocybe wasp induces the accumulation of reactive oxygen and phenolics in the host tree, Eucalypt.
gall induction is a multi-stage process, with egg oviposition being a crucial early step in gall formation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

egg deposition and oviposition by a gall-inducing wasps induces a range of plant responses including the oxidative burst, phenolic accumulation, cell division and the activation of a number of transcription factors.
gall-inducing wasps are capable of inducing a complex response in their host plants.
the egg and ovipositor fluid of a gall-forming wasp induce physiological and transcriptional changes in Eucalypt that are consistent with a response to attack and the initiation of gall development.
